pages_convention: XML section and paragraph locators (jats_text) for the abstract and captions. The XML text holds no body text, so body steps cite printed journal pages, which match PDF pages counted from 1 (pp. 1-16). Quotes from the body are copied from the PDF text.

entry.evidence: quantitative assessment of the runoff processes variations under 1.5 ◦C and 2 ◦C temperature rise in alpine regions is very important

steps.action: The authors take from Central Asian and Alpine studies the expectation that runoff increases more in basins with higher glacier ratios, with reported thresholds of 2%, 5% and 10%.
steps.quote: the higher the glacier ratio, the greater the increase in total runoff

steps.action: The authors pose the question of how runoff processes respond to warming in basins with different glacier ratios in the monsoon-influenced southern Tibetan Plateau, and state three objectives: component contributions, response with decreasing glacier ratio, and projection under 1.5 and 2 °C.
steps.quote: investigating the response mechanism of runoff process in basins with different glacier ratios would provide deeper insight into the effects of global warming

steps.action: The authors select five basins spanning glacier ratios of 20.7% to 1.8%, with similar monsoon climate and land-use gradients, as a space-for-time gradient that stands in for future glacier retreat.
steps.quote: changes in hydrological processes under future glacier retreat can be characterized to a certain extent by comparing runoff processes in these basins

steps.action: The authors assemble station precipitation and temperature (with a precipitation gradient for the ungauged Karuxung basin), DEM, land use, HWSD soils, the RGI glacier inventory, MODIS MOD10CM snow cover and observed discharge.
steps.quote: The MODIS monthly snow-cover (MOD10CM) product and runoff observation data shown in Fig. 1 were gathered to calibrate the parameters

steps.action: The authors calibrate the SPHY degree-day distributed model, with separate degree-day factors for debris-covered and debris-free ice, against observed monthly runoff and MODIS snow-cover area for 2000-2015.
steps.quote: Parameters of SPHY model were optimized to obtain reasonable hydrological simulation by comparing simulated monthly runoff and snow cover area (SCA)

steps.action: The authors check the model on a held-out validation period (1982-1999) with NSE, R2 and RMSE, compare simulated snow-cover area with MODIS, and benchmark the R2 values against ranges from previous alpine studies.
steps.quote: The model performance indicators for runoff simulation were found to be within acceptable ranges

steps.action: The authors decompose simulated historical runoff into base flow, glacier, snowmelt and rainfall runoff by basin, by 500 m elevation zone and by month, and find that the dominant component shifts with glacier ratio and altitude.
steps.quote: When the glacier ratio decreased from 20.7% to 13.5%, the main component of runoff shifted from glacier runoff to rainfall runoff.

steps.action: The authors compare historical trends of climate and runoff components across the basins (Table 2) and infer that temperature dominates runoff change above 13.5% glacier ratio and precipitation below 7.5%; they also estimate a 7-11 day advance of peak snowmelt.
steps.quote: It could be deduced that temperature may be the leading factor for runoff change in basins with glacier ratio higher than 13.5%

steps.action: The authors set the dominant-factor thresholds against studies from the Indus and the Tien Shan, and conclude that regional differences decide the dominance of temperature or precipitation.
steps.quote: Therefore, regional differences in the glacier ratio may determine the dominance of temperature or precipitation.

steps.action: The authors compute, from the multi-model ensemble mean of 25 CMIP6 GCMs, the years when warming of 1.5 °C and 2 °C relative to 1850-1900 is reached under four SSP scenarios.
steps.quote: According MME, the temperature rise of 1.5 ◦C will arrive in 2036, 2032, 2033, and 2029

steps.action: The authors compare the arrival times with previously published estimates and find them consistent.
steps.quote: Overall, the results of global temperature rise in this study are consistent with those of previous studies.

steps.action: The authors derive regional temperature and precipitation change (amplified relative to the global mean), Delta-downscale the GCM output, project glacier area with the MBG model, and drive the calibrated SPHY model to mid-century.
steps.quote: In general, the simulated total runoff and glacier runoff of each river basin showed an increasing trend under the four scenarios

steps.action: The authors compare the absence of peak glacier runoff by 1.5 and 2 °C with earlier projections and explain it by enhanced melt outweighing area loss.
steps.quote: [...] peak glacier runoff would not appear under global warming of 1.5 ◦C and 2 ◦C, which is supported by previous studies

steps.action: The authors attribute projected changes to runoff components (Table 3, Fig. 8) and compute monthly component changes relative to 1985-2014 at 1.5 °C (Fig. 9) and 2 °C (Fig. S8).
steps.quote: the driving factor of runoff increase in the future would change from glacier runoff to rainfall runoff with decreasing glacier ratio

steps.action: The authors state that the seasonal concentration of the runoff increase and the snowmelt decrease agree with earlier studies.
steps.quote: which are in accordance with the previous findings

steps.action: The authors compute the glacier regulation index (CV of total runoff over CV of non-glacier runoff) for basins and elevation zones and fit a power function of glacier ratio (R2 = 0.593).
steps.quote: GRI was calculated according to the definition described in 2.6 and the relationship between glacier ratio and GRI was then established.

steps.action: The authors set their GRI and glacier-ratio pattern against the GRI ranges reported by He et al. (2021) for other western Chinese basins and state that they agree.
steps.quote: The findings of this study also confirm this phenomenon.

steps.action: The authors project GRI for each basin under the four SSP scenarios and find that glacier regulation weakens as glaciers retreat.
steps.quote: The regulation function of glaciers will be attenuated along with the retreat of glaciers

steps.action: The authors keep four findings: a component shift with a glacier-ratio threshold, a glacier contribution more than twice the glacier ratio, projected trends in the components, and a power-law GRI relation with weakening regulation.
steps.quote: The major runoff component shifted from glacier runoff to rainfall runoff when the glacier ratio decreased, and the critical threshold was between 20% and 13.5%.

end.claim: Across basins with glacier ratios of 1.8-20.7% in the monsoon-influenced southern Tibetan Plateau, runoff composition and the glacier hydrological regulation function scale with glacier ratio, and under 1.5 and 2 °C warming total, glacier, rainfall and base-flow runoff increase while snowmelt runoff decreases and glacier regulation weakens.

decisive_move.sentence: Calibrating SPHY to observed runoff and MODIS snow cover and using it to separate runoff into glacier, snowmelt, rainfall and base-flow components is what makes every component share, trend, GRI value and projection possible.

gates.evidence: The basins were chosen to span a glacier-ratio gradient (p. 3) to answer a question, not to test a stated hypothesis; the expectation cited from Kaldybayev et al. and Birsan et al. is not tested as such. The model faced a held-out validation period it could have failed (Fig. 3; p. 6). The component shares, dominant-factor thresholds, GRI relation (R2 = 0.593) and projections faced no test that could falsify them. Nothing was fixed before the data.

limits: The XML text holds only the abstract and captions, so all body steps cite printed pages. The supplement (Figs. S1-S8, Table S1, GCM selection rule) was not supplied. The PDF captions of Fig. 2 and Fig. 3 appear swapped relative to the plotted content: Fig. 2 shows runoff NSE and R2, Fig. 3 shows SCA against MODIS (inference from the page images). The Lhasa glacier ratio is 1.8% in Table 1 but 2.0% in §3.2.1 and Fig. 4. The text on p. 8 cites Table 3 where the historical trends are in Table 2. The abstract's ranges (for example total runoff 1.7-20.6%) differ from the 1.5 °C ranges on p. 11 (1.7-16.0%); presumably they include 2 °C (Fig. S8, not seen). MODIS SCA was used both to calibrate and to verify, so the SCA comparison is not independent. Sub-claims and their status: (a) the projected component changes are scenario projections from a GCM ensemble mean with no reported uncertainty bounds, so they fall short of estimate_with_resolution (status: none as an estimate); (b) the temperature-dominant and precipitation-dominant thresholds (above 13.5%, below 7.5%) rest on five basins and are stated as deductions (best_explanation at most); (c) the GRI power law (R2 = 0.593) mixes basins and their own elevation zones, which are not independent cases (regularity_in_range, weak); (d) the claim that results transfer to the Andes, Central Asia and Europe (p. 13) is asserted, not tested. No sensitivity tests of SPHY parameters, the downscaling method, the glacier-retreat assumption or GCM spread are reported. Permafrost and vegetation change are acknowledged as omitted (p. 13). Data are not shared (p. 15). No review file was supplied. The entry could also be coded external_goal, since the Paris Agreement targets frame the scenarios (coder judgement).

disagreements.target: Sorg et al. (2012), Tien Shan basins
disagreements.support: Sorg et al. found temperature dominant in a basin with 5% glacier ratio, against this study's finding that precipitation dominates below 7.5%; the authors attribute the difference to regional factors rather than resolving it.
disagreements.quote: However, studies in Tien Shan (Central Asia) indicated that temperature strongly affects runoff in basins with a glacier ratio of 5%

disagreements.target: Consensus that glaciers with wider coverage have stronger effects on runoff (Liu et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2022)
disagreements.support: The authors argue that climate and topography, besides glacier ratio, complicate the dominant control, citing differing thresholds across regions; they offer no new test.
disagreements.quote: [...] factor influencing runoff would be complicated in alpine regions because of the significant differences in physical properties

alternatives_considered.reason: statistical downscaling has good transferability and efficient computation

alternatives_considered.chosen: Changes reported relative to both the preindustrial era (1850-1900) and the present-day period (1985-2014)
alternatives_considered.reason: it is more practical to compare future climate change with the present-day conditions

alternatives_considered.chosen: Multi-model ensemble mean of 25 CMIP6 GCMs
alternatives_considered.reason: multi-model ensemble means are more consistent with observations than a single model (citing Mote and Salathé, 2010)
